domains.name: Self-Knowledge: The Humanmetrics Assessment
domains.summary: The Jung-typology assessment as a self-knowledge instrument: what it measures, what it doesn't, and how to convert a type into career fit and a development plan — independent study, no affiliation with any assessment provider.

scenarios.title: The hiring-screen misuse
scenarios.situation: A hiring manager asks candidates to take the Jung typology test and rejects everyone who doesn't test as ENTJ — 'we only hire commanders.' You know the instrument: 72 forced-choice questions sorting preferences across four dichotomies (Extraversion/Introversion, Sensing/Intuition, Thinking/Feeling, Judging/Perceiving) into 16 types.
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with using the assessment this way?
choices: The instrument measures preferences — how people prefer to take in information and make decisions — not ability, competence, or job performance; using it as a hiring filter is both a misuse of what it measures and unfair to candidates whose strengths lie outside one type.
Nothing is wrong; ENTJs are objectively the best leaders so the filter is efficient.
The only problem is the 72-question length; a shorter test would make the filter fine.
The problem is that candidates can lie; with a lie-detector version the filter would work.
scenarios.why: Preference is not performance: an INTJ and an ESFP can both be excellent engineers, and the test says nothing about skill, experience, or motivation. The instrument's own design purpose is self-knowledge for development and career reflection — converting it into a hiring gate confuses 'how someone prefers to work' with 'whether they can do the work,' and it screens out strong candidates for no valid reason.
scenarios.hint: Does the test measure what you CAN do, or what you PREFER?

scenarios.title: Reading your own result
scenarios.situation: Your assessment result reads: INTJ — Introverted (38%), Intuitive (3%), Thinking (6%), Judging (38%). The write-up calls INTJs 'systems builders' who prize competence and independence. You're excited, but two of the four preferences are marginal — nearly 50/50.
scenarios.prompt: How should you interpret the marginal preferences?
choices: Treat the percentages as preference clarity, not as grades: a 3% Intuition preference means characteristics of both INTJ and ISTJ may apply to you — work with the whole profile including the near-ties, not just the four-letter label.
Ignore the percentages; the four letters are definitive and the numbers are decoration.
Retake the test until all four preferences are strong, then trust the result.
The marginal scores mean the test failed and the result should be discarded.
scenarios.why: The percentage is the strength of the preference signal on that sitting: 38% is moderate clarity, 3% is essentially no preference. Near-tie dimensions mean you genuinely draw on both sides — planning with the ISTJ description alongside the INTJ one gives a truer picture than the label alone. The working-styles view uses the full profile; the four letters are just shorthand.
scenarios.hint: If Intuition is 3%, which other type's description is worth reading too?

scenarios.title: Type to role-family mapping
scenarios.situation: A career counselor maps your ISTJ result — Introverted, Sensing, Thinking, Judging — to role families. The write-up describes ISTJs as thorough, dependable, practical, and organized, thriving on clear processes and schedules. You're choosing between two offers: site-reliability operations with strict runbooks, and developer-evangelist doing conference talks and demos.
scenarios.prompt: Which fit does the type suggest, and with what caveat?
choices: The ISTJ working style aligns with the SRE operations role — structured processes, reliability, checklists, deep focus — while the evangelist role leans on extraverted, spontaneous strengths; the caveat is that type suggests energy fit and working style, not capability — you could succeed at either, but one will cost less daily energy.
Take the evangelist role; type is meaningless so either choice is identical.
ISTJs must never take public-facing roles under any circumstances.
The type determines your ceiling; pick the role matching your type or fail.
scenarios.why: Type-to-role mapping is about sustainable energy, not permission: structured, process-driven operations rewards exactly the ISTJ strengths (thoroughness, dependability, love of order), while constant public performance taxes introverted preferences daily. Both are doable — the question is which role leaves you energized at 6pm. Use the map to predict friction, not to forbid ambition.
scenarios.hint: Which role rewards checklists and deep focus, and which rewards stage presence?

scenarios.title: Composing the founding team
scenarios.situation: You're assembling a three-person founding team and have four candidates' type profiles: an INTJ systems architect, an ENFP evangelist, an ISTJ operator, and an ESTP hustler who thrives in chaos. You can only pick three, and the startup needs product depth, customer energy, and operational discipline in its first year.
scenarios.prompt: What composition principle should guide the pick?
choices: Cover the three working-style bases with complementary strengths — architect (INTJ) for product depth, evangelist (ENFP) for customer energy, operator (ISTJ) for discipline — and manage the known friction points explicitly (e.g., the INTJ's impatience with process vs. the ISTJ's need for it) rather than hoping chemistry handles it.
Pick the three highest-IQ candidates regardless of type; intelligence dominates team outcomes.
Pick three of the same type for maximum alignment and zero friction.
Pick whoever is available first; team composition is overthinking.
scenarios.why: Diverse working styles cover more of the startup's demands than any single profile: the INTJ designs the system, the ENFP sells the vision, the ISTJ keeps the machine running. The value of the typology here is predictive — naming the friction before it happens (independence vs. process, big-picture vs. detail) so the team designs working agreements around it instead of discovering it in a crisis.
scenarios.hint: Which startup job goes unfilled if you drop the ISTJ?

scenarios.title: What it doesn't measure
scenarios.situation: A colleague dismisses the whole instrument: 'It's astrology for HR. It doesn't predict job performance, test-retest reliability is imperfect, and the dichotomies are really continuous traits.' They conclude the assessment is worthless for career planning.
scenarios.prompt: What is the accurate middle position?
choices: The criticisms are substantially true — it measures preferences not abilities, the cutoffs are dichotomized continua, and it shouldn't gate hiring — but 'not predictive of performance' doesn't mean 'useless for self-knowledge': as a structured mirror for working style, energy, and blind spots, it earns its place in career reflection alongside skills audits and market data.
The colleague is entirely wrong; the test is scientifically airtight and predicts everything.
The colleague is entirely right; burn the result and never think about working style again.
The test is valid only for extroverts; introverts should use a different instrument.
scenarios.why: Intellectual honesty requires conceding the limits: preferences are not competencies, the four dichotomies slice continuous dimensions, and retest drift happens. But the instrument was never a performance predictor — it's a vocabulary for self-knowledge. Knowing you recharge alone, decide by logic, and need closure before acting is actionable career information even if no peer-reviewed paper blesses the 16 boxes. Use it as one input, never the verdict.
scenarios.hint: If it doesn't predict performance, what CAN it legitimately inform?

scenarios.title: The development plan
scenarios.situation: Your profile is INTJ with strong Thinking and Judging: you decide fast by logic, love systems, and find open-ended emotional conversations draining. Your new role requires leading a team through an ambiguous reorg — exactly the zone your non-preferred side (Feeling, Perceiving) governs: sitting with uncertainty, attuning to people's anxieties, holding plans loosely.
scenarios.prompt: How do you build the development plan?
choices: Name the specific non-preferred muscles the role demands, design low-stakes reps (weekly 1:1s focused on listening not solving, written decision logs that stay open to revision), set observable markers (team reports feeling heard), and review monthly — developing the weaker side while leading from your strengths, not pretending the preferences flipped.
Retake the test until you get ENFJ, then lead naturally.
Avoid the Feeling/Perceiving demands entirely; delegate all people work forever.
Announce to the team that you're an INTJ so they lower their expectations.
scenarios.why: Type development means strengthening the non-preferred functions deliberately, not rewiring your personality: the INTJ's systems thinking becomes the scaffold (structured 1:1s, explicit feedback loops) inside which the weaker muscles get reps. The plan is behavioral and measurable — listening reps, revision-tolerant plans, feedback markers — because 'be more empathetic' is a wish, not a plan.
scenarios.hint: What is one observable marker that your listening reps are working?

scenarios.title: The Two Tests
scenarios.situation: A client's Big Five shows very high Conscientiousness but their Humanmetrics result is P with 80% clarity. They conclude one test is 'wrong.'
evidence: Big Five: very high C; Humanmetrics: P at 80% clarity.
choices: The divergence is information, not error: high conscientiousness (diligent, reliable trait) can coexist with a P preference (keeping options open, flexible process) — the Big Five measures the trait outcome, the type instrument measures the preferred process. This person is reliably diligent AND prefers open-ended workflow — the combination (disciplined improviser) is a real pattern the single-system view would miss. Two lenses, stereoscopic depth.
One test is wrong; discard it.
Average them into ambiversion.
Retake both until they agree.
scenarios.hint: High Big Five Conscientiousness coexists with a P preference — is one test wrong?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It explains the coexistence mechanistically (trait outcome vs preferred process) and names the combined pattern — the stereoscopic payoff. B/C/D all collapse the depth.

scenarios.title: The Translated Item
scenarios.situation: A multinational team takes the test in three languages. The Japanese team's F scores are markedly higher than the US team's — HR concludes the Japanese team is 'more feeling.'
evidence: 3 languages; Japanese team F markedly higher; HR: 'more feeling.'
choices: Multiple confounds before conclusions: translation shifts (items' emotional language landing differently), cultural expressiveness norms (collectivist harmony-values inflating F-item endorsement), and possibly real preference differences — inseparable from the scores alone. The cautious move: treat the pattern as 'tell me more' (best-fit conversations in each culture's idiom), never as a finding about the teams. HR's conclusion leaps past all three confounds.
HR is right; the data is clear.
The Japanese team is mistyped.
Only the US results count.
scenarios.hint: Translated administrations show team F-score gaps — what is the cautious reading?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It enumerates the confounds (translation, norms, real difference — inseparable), prescribes the cautious method (best-fit conversations), and blocks the leap. B/C/D all leap or dismiss.

scenarios.title: The Defensive Client
scenarios.situation: A coaching client arrives defensive: 'I know what this is — corporate astrology. My company made me take it.' They scored ESTJ.
choices: Validate then reframe: honor the skepticism (it's partly earned — the validity debate is real, and mandated testing breeds resistance), then offer the developmental frame ('forget the company; is there anything here about how you operate that you'd find useful?') — and run the protocol on THEIR terms: their story first, the Barnum guard explicitly ('let's check the falsifiable parts together'), ending with one growth edge THEY choose. Resistance met with honesty becomes engagement.
Insist the test is scientific.
Agree it's astrology; skip it.
Type them harder to prove it.
scenarios.hint: A defensive mandated client calls it 'corporate astrology' — how should the coach open?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It validates the earned skepticism, offers the invitational frame, applies the Barnum guard collaboratively, and ends with client-chosen development — resistance converted through honesty. B/C/D all mishandle.

scenarios.title: The Empty Journal
scenarios.situation: A student buys a beautiful journal for type observations, writes three elaborate entries, then abandons it — 'I don't have time for this.'
choices: Shrink the practice until it's un-abandonable: five lines, five minutes, the template — the elaborate entries were the failure mode (friction kills practice; perfectionism kills honesty). The journal that survives is the ugly, brief, honest one — grip Tuesdays and all. Design for the tired Tuesday, not the inspired Sunday.
Buy a nicer journal.
Journaling isn't for everyone.
Write longer entries less often.
scenarios.hint: An elaborate journal is abandoned in three entries — what is the correction?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It diagnoses the failure mode (elaborate-entry friction), prescribes the minimal survivable practice, and states the design principle (tired-Tuesday, not inspired-Sunday) — the P-compatible correction from the practices topic, applied. B/C/D all miss.

scenarios.title: The Retired Executive
scenarios.situation: A retired executive (career-long ENTJ) retests at 68 and gets INFP — and is distressed: 'Have I been faking my whole life?'
evidence: career ENTJ; age 68 retired; retests INFP; distressed.
choices: Neither faking nor transformation: the career trained Te-Ni relentlessly (the J-mask of executive demand) while retirement lifted the closure-pressure — and the lifespan sequence (tertiary Fi maturing, inferior... the values and reflectiveness emerging) finally has room. The ENTJ years were real competence; the INFP result is the disinhibited preference plus developed feeling. Both true; the distress comes from the identity-story, not the data.
They were faking; the truth emerges.
The test is wrong; ignore it.
Retirees can't be typed.
scenarios.hint: A lifelong ENTJ retests INFP at 68 — 'was I faking?' — what is the wise response?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It honors both results (trained competence + disinhibited preference + development), explains the mechanism (mask lifted, tertiary maturing), and locates the distress in the story not the data. B/C/D all collapse.

scenarios.title: The Compatibility Report
scenarios.situation: A couple pays for a 'type compatibility report' that rates them 34% compatible ('challenging match') — they're distressed despite three good years together.
evidence: paid report: 34% 'challenging'; couple: 3 good years, distressed.
choices: The evidence hierarchy: three good years are data; the 34% is unevidenced arithmetic (no outcome studies behind the number — it's theory-aesthetics monetized). The response: refund the authority to the relationship (study what actually works between you), use the report's friction section if useful (the protocols are the honest part), and discard the score. The chart doesn't get a vote on the lived relationship.
The report knows best; reconsider.
They're incompatible; the years were luck.
Buy the advanced report.
scenarios.hint: A 34% compatibility score distresses a happy couple — what is the response?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It establishes the evidence hierarchy (lived years over unevidenced score), explains the number's emptiness, salvages the useful part (friction protocols), and returns authority to the relationship. B/C/D all crown the chart.

scenarios.title: The Self-Knowledge: The Humanmetrics Assessment Mystery
scenarios.situation: Users report that Self-Knowledge: The Humanmetrics Assessment is not working correctly. The obvious checks pass — the components are online, basic connectivity works. You need to think in systems, not symptoms.
scenarios.prompt: Using the systems anatomy method (whole → cut open → step through → pull apart), how would you systematically trace a failure in Self-Knowledge: The Humanmetrics Assessment?
choices: Walk the full journey: start from the trigger, verify each handoff in sequence, check dependencies at every step, and isolate where the flow breaks — then examine that specific layer
Restart all components — Self-Knowledge: The Humanmetrics Assessment issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately
Escalate to senior support — Self-Knowledge: The Humanmetrics Assessment is too complex to troubleshoot systematically
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Systems thinking means tracing the living flow: (1) Whole: what is Self-Knowledge: The Humanmetrics Assessment supposed to do end-to-end? (2) Cut open: what are the layers/stages? (3) Step through: verify each handoff — where does the expected output diverge from actual? (4) Pull apart: isolate the broken layer and examine it in detail. This method works for any Self-Knowledge: The Humanmetrics Assessment failure in Humanmetrics.
scenarios.hint: Don't jump to the fix. First map the journey, then find where it breaks.
objectives: Apply systems anatomy to Self-Knowledge: The Humanmetrics Assessment
evidence: All Self-Knowledge: The Humanmetrics Assessment components report 'online'. Basic health checks pass.
Functionality is broken despite green status indicators. The failure is in the flow, not the components.

domains.name: Jungian Foundations
domains.description: Jung's Psychological Types: attitudes, functions, and the architecture of the psyche.

scenarios.title: The Pop-Jung Quote
scenarios.situation: A team workshop opens with a slide: 'Jung said there are 16 personality types, each suited to specific careers.' The facilitator presents this as Jung's own finding.
evidence: Jung 1921: attitudes/functions; 16 types: Briggs-Myers; careers: later practitioners.
choices: Jung never described 16 types or career matching — he described attitudes and functions; the 16-type framework and the instrument are Briggs-Myers (and later) developments, and career mapping came later still. The quote backdates three layers of development onto Jung himself.
Nothing — Jung invented the 16 types.
Jung described 8 types, close enough.
The facilitator should have cited Humanmetrics instead.
scenarios.hint: A workshop credits Jung with the 16 types and career matching — what is the historical error?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It separates the layers: Jung (attitudes/functions, 1921), Briggs-Myers (16 types, instrument), later practitioners (career mapping). Collapsing them misattributes and misunderstands — the 16-type system is an operationalization, not Jung's text. B and C misstate the history; D swaps one misattribution for another.

scenarios.title: The 'Wrong' Result
scenarios.situation: A test-taker scores 52% Introversion and concludes the test is broken — 'I'm not really an introvert, I like people.' They want to retake it until they get a 'clear' result.
choices: A near-middle score is a valid result indicating flexibility or situational variation — the preference is slight, and both orientations are available. 'Liking people' was never the question; the scale measures energy orientation. Retaking until a strong result appears manufactures false clarity.
The test is broken; retake until it's clear.
They're definitely an extravert in denial.
Average the retakes for the real type.
scenarios.hint: A 52% I score feels 'wrong' to a sociable test-taker — what is the accurate reading?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It normalizes the mid-range result (flexibility, not failure), corrects the construct misunderstanding (energy, not sociability), and warns against clarity-shopping through retakes. B surrenders to the misconception; C pathologizes; D averages noise into false precision.

scenarios.title: The 'Emotional' Feeler
scenarios.situation: A manager says: 'We can't put her on the analytics project — she's a Feeler, too emotional for data.' The team member has strong quantitative skills and a Feeling preference.
evidence: Feeling-preference analyst with strong quant skills denied project.
choices: Conflating feeling with emotion (Jung's feeling is rational valuing, not emotionality) and conflating preference with ability (a Feeling preference says nothing about quantitative skill). The decision discriminates on a double misunderstanding — the relevant question is her analytics ability, which the type doesn't measure.
The manager is right to be cautious.
Feelers should avoid analytics.
Retype her as a Thinker.
scenarios.hint: A 'Feeler' is blocked from analytics as 'too emotional' — what are the two errors?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It names both confusions precisely — the technical meaning of feeling and the preference/ability distinction — and redirects to the relevant criterion (actual skill). This is also a legal/ethical point: using type results for discriminatory placement is misuse. B, C endorse the errors; D manipulates the instrument.

scenarios.title: The Type as Excuse
scenarios.situation: Someone with a Thinking preference says: 'I'm a T — I can't help being blunt; feelings just aren't my thing.' They use the type to excuse hurting colleagues and refuse feedback.
evidence: 'I'm a T, can't help it' used to deflect feedback repeatedly.
scenarios.prompt: What is the mature response to this?
choices: Type describes preferences, not permissions: a Thinking preference explains why tact takes effort, not why it's optional — and the shadow/inferior-function work (developing feeling) is precisely the growth the theory prescribes. Using type as an excuse inverts its purpose, which is self-knowledge in service of development.
They're right; Ts can't do tact.
Retype them until they're an F.
Types shouldn't be discussed at work.
scenarios.hint: A Thinker uses type to excuse bluntness — what is the mature reading?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It holds both truths — the preference is real (tact takes effort) and the excuse is invalid (effort is still required) — and points to the theory's actual prescription (develop the inferior). B endorses the excuse; C manipulates; D abandons the tool because of its misuse.

scenarios.title: The Fixed Identity
scenarios.situation: A test-taker frames their result as 'I discovered who I really am' and begins filtering all decisions through it — career, relationships, hobbies must all 'fit the type.' Five years pass; the identity hardens.
evidence: 'I AM an INTJ' filtering all life decisions; 5 years, no growth edges pursued.
scenarios.prompt: What is the healthier relationship to the result?
choices: Hold it as a snapshot of current preferences and a map of growth edges: the type describes habitual patterns AND points to the less-preferred functions as the development direction. Identity-hardening around four letters arrests the very development (individuation) the theory exists to serve.
The identity is correct; lean in harder.
Retake yearly to update the identity.
Types are meaningless; discard it.
scenarios.hint: A type result hardens into a fixed identity — what is the healthier stance?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It preserves the result's value (pattern recognition, growth direction) while refusing the identity-freeze — the theory's own developmental model (individuation) contradicts fixed-type identity. B endorses the arrest; C treats development as re-measurement; D discards the tool with its misuse.

scenarios.title: The Meaningful Coincidence
scenarios.situation: A test-taker experiences a striking coincidence the week after learning their type and concludes the universe is confirming their result — 'I was meant to be an INFJ.'
evidence: 'the universe confirmed my INFJ' after a striking coincidence.
choices: Honor the experience without inflating the inference: meaningful coincidences are psychologically significant (they mark moments of attention and transition) without being evidential for the type result — the test stands or falls on its psychometrics, not on cosmic confirmation. Jung himself distinguished the experience's meaning from its explanatory status.
The universe confirmed it; trust the type absolutely.
Coincidences are meaningless; ignore it.
Retake the test during coincidences for accuracy.
scenarios.hint: A coincidence after the test feels like cosmic confirmation — what is the balanced view?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It validates the experience's psychological significance while refusing the evidential leap — the exact balance Jung's own writing models. B inflates; C dismisses what Jung considered meaningful; D is superstitious procedure.

domains.name: The Eight Cognitive Functions
domains.description: The eight function-attitudes (Te, Ti, Fe, Fi, Se, Si, Ne, Ni) and how they actually operate.

scenarios.title: The Efficiency Audit
scenarios.situation: A Te-dominant manager optimizes the team's workflow: ticket quotas rise 40%, handle time drops. Three months later, two top performers quit citing burnout, and quality complaints spike.
evidence: tickets +40%, handle time down; 3 months: 2 quits, quality complaints up.
scenarios.prompt: What does the function analysis say went wrong?
choices: Te optimized the measurable (throughput, handle time) while its blind spot — the human cost of efficiency — went unmanaged: 'what works' was defined without the people running the process. The fix isn't less Te (the system-building is valuable) but Te informed by feeling-values: sustainable pace, quality, morale as first-class metrics.
Te is wrong for management.
The quitters were the wrong type.
More metrics would have prevented this.
scenarios.hint: A Te optimization boosts throughput but burns out the team — what is the function-level diagnosis?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It diagnoses the classic Te blind spot precisely and prescribes the integration (feeling-values as metrics) rather than abandoning the function. B discards a strength; C blames the victims; D doubles down on the blind spot.

scenarios.title: The Analysis That Never Ships
scenarios.situation: A Ti-dominant analyst has spent six weeks refining a forecasting model's theoretical foundations. The business needed a directional answer in two weeks; the opportunity window is closing.
evidence: 6 weeks refining; business needed directional answer in 2.
choices: Borrow Te: timebox the analysis, ship the 'good enough' directional model now, and schedule the refinement as a v2 — Ti's depth is the asset, but closure is the skill to develop. The prescription honors the function (the rigor is real value) while addressing the blind spot (practical closure) directly.
Ti is unsuited to business.
More time will perfect it.
Hand the model to someone else.
scenarios.hint: A Ti analyst's perfect model misses the business window — what is the prescription?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It prescribes the specific integration (Te-style closure: timebox, ship, iterate) while honoring Ti's genuine contribution — development, not replacement. B discards the strength; C feeds the blind spot; D avoids the growth.

scenarios.title: The Swallowed Objection
scenarios.situation: An Fe-dominant team member senses a plan is flawed but stays silent to preserve harmony. The plan fails; afterward they say 'I knew it wouldn't work.'
evidence: flawed plan failed; Fe-user: 'I knew it wouldn't work.'
choices: Fe's harmony-seeking has a failure mode: self-erasure that harms the group it aims to protect — the objection, delivered kindly and early, IS the harmonious act. Mature Fe includes one's own perceptions as legitimate group data; 'what do people need?' includes the truth they need to hear.
Fe is unsuited to leadership.
They should have stayed silent; harmony matters most.
Fe-users can't assess plans.
scenarios.hint: An Fe-user's silence 'for harmony' lets a flawed plan fail — what is the lesson?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It reframes the mature form (the kindly-delivered objection as the truly harmonious act) and names the blind spot's irony (protecting the group by withholding from it). B discards; C endorses the failure mode; D confuses function with competence.

scenarios.title: The Values Collision
scenarios.situation: An Fi-dominant employee refuses to work on a project they consider unethical. The Fe-dominant manager sees a team player abandoning the team in a crunch.
evidence: Fi: 'unethical project'; Fe manager: 'abandoning the team.'
choices: Take the Fi conviction seriously (it's data about the project's ethics, possibly the canary in the coal mine) while requiring the Fe concern be addressed (the team's crunch is real) — reassign the employee, and investigate the ethical concern rather than dismissing it. Both functions are reporting something true; the resolution honors the value and the relationship.
Fi is insubordination; discipline them.
Fe is compromise; ignore the manager.
Values have no place at work.
scenarios.hint: An Fi refusal collides with an Fe team crunch — what is the resolution?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It treats both functions as information sources (the ethical canary, the real crunch) and resolves practically (reassign + investigate) — honoring value and relationship simultaneously. B punishes conscience; C dismisses the team; D abandons the domain.

scenarios.title: The Missed Future
scenarios.situation: An Se-dominant sales star consistently wins the quarter but never builds the pipeline — every period starts from zero. The pattern repeats for three years.
evidence: 3 years: wins the quarter, pipeline always at zero.
choices: Borrow Ni/Si: the Se strength (closing in the present) is real and valuable, but the blind spot (the longer arc) needs scaffolding — a pipeline ritual, a future-review habit, a system that converts present wins into future position. Development adds the missing temporal orientation without dulling the present-tense gift.
Se is unsuited to sales.
More present-focus will fix it.
Accept the cycle as the type's fate.
scenarios.hint: An Se star wins quarters but never builds pipeline — what is the prescription?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It prescribes the specific development (scaffolding the longer arc: pipeline rituals, future review) while honoring the gift — the classic individuation move of adding the less-preferred orientation. B discards; C feeds the blind spot; D fatalizes.

scenarios.title: The Needed Change
scenarios.situation: An Si-dominant operations lead resists a new system: 'The old process works; we've used it for a decade.' The old process is genuinely failing under new scale — error rates have tripled.
evidence: old process: decade of use; error rates tripled under new scale.
scenarios.prompt: How should the change be approached?
choices: Work WITH Si, not against it: honor the decade of reliability (the old process earned its trust), present the new system as the updated precedent (pilot data, the documented why), and give Si the detailed transition plan it needs. Si resists the unproven, not the proven-better — make the new system's reliability demonstrable and the resistance becomes diligence.
Si is obstruction; override them.
The old process is sacred; keep it.
Replace the operations lead.
scenarios.hint: An Si lead resists a failing old process — how should change be approached?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It works with the function's logic (Si trusts the demonstrated, so demonstrate) rather than pathologizing it — and reframes the resistance as diligence once the new system's reliability is shown. B/C/D all mishandle: override, surrender, or remove.

scenarios.title: The Ten Open Loops
scenarios.situation: An Ne-dominant founder has ten initiatives open, all exciting, none finished. The team is exhausted by the pivots; the runway is burning.
evidence: 10 initiatives open, none finished; team exhausted; runway burning.
choices: Borrow Si/J: the Ne generativity is the company's asset (the ideas are genuinely good), but the blind spot (closure) needs structure — a finisher partner, a 'three bets' rule, explicit loop-closing rituals. The intervention adds the missing orientation (follow-through scaffolding) without killing the generative engine.
Ne is unsuited to founding.
More ideas will save the company.
Shut down all but one initiative permanently.
scenarios.hint: An Ne founder's ten open loops are burning the runway — what is the intervention?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It protects the asset (generativity) while scaffolding the blind spot (closure structures: finisher partner, bet limits, rituals) — development, not suppression. B discards; C feeds the blind spot; D is blunt-force that kills the engine.

scenarios.title: The Wrong Vision
scenarios.situation: An Ni-dominant executive commits the company to a vision with total certainty. Two years in, the market data contradicts it — but the executive dismisses the data as 'noise' and doubles down.
evidence: 2 years committed; market data contradicts; dismissed as 'noise.'
scenarios.prompt: What went wrong at the function level?
choices: Ni's blind spot (present data) metastasized: the converging vision, normally the executive's gift, became unfalsifiable — contradictory evidence relabeled as noise. The correction is Se's discipline (what are the facts on the ground?) institutionalized as premortems, red teams, and kill criteria set BEFORE the vision's emotional investment peaks.
Ni is dangerous and should be suppressed.
The executive needed more confidence.
Visions should never be questioned.
scenarios.hint: An Ni executive's vision becomes unfalsifiable — what went wrong and what corrects it?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It diagnoses the specific failure mode (vision become unfalsifiable) and prescribes the structural correction (premortems, red teams, pre-set kill criteria) — Se's discipline institutionalized. B suppresses the gift; C/D feed the pathology.

domains.name: The Four Dichotomies
domains.description: E/I, S/N, T/F, J/P — what each scale measures, how scores work, and how to read them.

scenarios.title: The Trained Extravert
scenarios.situation: A sales director scores I with 85% clarity. They're the life of every client dinner, run a 200-person org, and insist the test is wrong — 'I'm obviously an extravert.'
evidence: I 85% clarity; 15-year sales director; 'obviously an extravert.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely explanation?
choices: Practiced behavior masking preference: fifteen years of sales trained superb extraverted skills, but the clarity score (85%) suggests the instrument consistently detected the underlying recharge pattern — they're likely an introvert with excellent trained extraversion who recharges alone. The question isn't the client-dinner performance (skill) but the Sunday morning (energy).
The test is definitely wrong.
They're lying on the items.
Extraverts can't score I.
scenarios.hint: A star sales director scores I at 85% clarity but insists they're extraverted — what is the likely explanation?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It applies the skill/preference distinction and takes the clarity score seriously as evidence — the trained-extravert mistype is the classic pattern. B surrenders; C impugns; D states a false rule.

scenarios.title: The Evasive Report
scenarios.situation: A Sensing VP keeps rejecting an Intuitive analyst's reports: 'Too theoretical — what actually happened?' The analyst feels the VP is anti-intellectual; the VP feels the analyst is evasive.
scenarios.prompt: What is happening and what fixes it?
choices: An S/N information-diet mismatch: the analyst leads with patterns (N habit), the VP needs the concrete sequence first (S habit) — each misreads the other (evasive vs anti-intellectual). The fix is translation protocol: concrete example first, then the pattern and its implication. Neither needs to change their mind, only their order of presentation.
The analyst is too theoretical.
The VP is anti-intellectual.
Reassign the analyst.
scenarios.hint: A Sensing VP and Intuitive analyst misread each other — what is the dynamic and the fix?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It diagnoses the diet mismatch without moralizing either side and prescribes the minimal effective change (order of presentation) — translation, not conversion. B/C take sides in the misreading; D avoids the growth.

scenarios.title: The 'Too Emotional' Label
scenarios.situation: A Feeling-preference manager's decision is dismissed in a meeting: 'That's emotional, let's be logical about this.' The decision was actually a values-based analysis of stakeholder impact.
choices: The dismissal confuses the criterion with temperature: a values-based stakeholder analysis IS a rationality — it evaluates by legitimate criteria (impact on people, fairness, trust) that impersonal logic misses. The reframe: 'This is a values-based analysis: the stakeholder impact is X, which affects Y outcome.' Translate the criterion into legitimacy language rather than accepting the 'emotional' frame.
The manager was being emotional.
Feelings don't belong in decisions.
The manager should have hidden the values.
scenarios.hint: A values-based decision is dismissed as 'emotional' — what is the reframe?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It refuses the temperature frame, asserts the criterion's rationality with specifics, and gives the translation move — the practical defense against the scale's weaponization. B/C accept the misframe; D counsels concealment.

scenarios.title: The Vacation Standoff
scenarios.situation: A J partner wants the vacation fully booked by March; a P partner wants to 'see how we feel in July.' The J calls it irresponsible; the P calls it controlling. The fight repeats yearly.
choices: Name the closure-needs mismatch (not a character dispute) and negotiate the decide-by structure: book the non-negotiables early (flights, the J's closure need) with explicit open zones (the P's exploration need) and a final decide-by date for the rest. Both get their need met structurally — the J's planning and the P's openness stop being moral positions and become design parameters.
The J should relax.
The P should grow up.
Vacation separately.
scenarios.hint: A J/P couple fights yearly over vacation planning — what resolves it?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It de-moralizes the conflict (needs, not character) and designs the structural solution (booked anchors + open zones + decide-by date) that satisfies both closure needs. B/C moralize one side; D avoids.

scenarios.title: The Clarity Shopper
scenarios.situation: A test-taker scores N-53 and retakes the test four times, answering more extremely each time, until they get N-81 — 'now it's clear I'm intuitive.'
choices: Clarity-shopping manufactures false precision: the original 53% was the honest measurement (low clarity = genuinely balanced/flexible on S/N), and the 81% is an artifact of extreme answering, not a truer self. The retakes didn't discover the preference; they distorted the instrument. The middle was the answer.
Nothing — clearer is better.
They should retake a fifth time.
The first result was broken.
scenarios.hint: A test-taker retakes until N-53 becomes N-81 — what is wrong?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It names the mechanism (extreme answering distorts the instrument) and defends the original measurement — the middle as honest answer. This is the clarity-shopping prohibition applied. B/C endorse the distortion; D misdiagnoses.

scenarios.title: The Aspirational Answers
scenarios.situation: A test-taker admires decisive leaders, answers every item as the bold decisive self they aspire to be, and gets ENTJ. Their colleagues would describe them as reflective, accommodating, and spontaneous — ENFP patterns.
evidence: self-report ENTJ vs observer ENFP patterns.
scenarios.prompt: What happened and what is the remedy?
choices: Aspiration mistype: the test measured the admired self, not the habitual — the instrument can't distinguish them; only honesty can. The remedy is the best-fit process: retake answering as 'typically me on an ordinary Tuesday' (not the ideal), read both ENTJ and ENFP descriptions, and let the colleagues' observations weigh in. The honest result is more useful than the admired one.
They're an ENTJ now; aspiration becomes reality.
The colleagues are wrong.
Take a different test.
scenarios.hint: Aspirational answering yields ENTJ; colleagues see ENFP — what happened and what is the remedy?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It names the mechanism (admired vs habitual self), gives the concrete retake instruction (ordinary-Tuesday framing), and invokes best-fit with outside observers — the full professional remedy. B confuses aspiration with identity; C dismisses data; D avoids.

domains.name: The Sixteen Types
domains.description: Profiles of the 16 types: gifts, blind spots, and how to recognize each in the wild.

scenarios.title: The Competence Clash
scenarios.situation: An INTJ architect and an ESFJ manager collide: the architect calls the team's process 'irrational,' the manager calls the architect 'impossible to work with.' Both are performing well by their own lights.
evidence: INTJ: 'irrational process' vs ESFJ: 'impossible to work with.'
choices: An NT/SF values collision: the INTJ evaluates by coherence/efficiency (Ni-Te) and experiences the process as the problem; the ESFJ evaluates by harmony/continuity (Fe-Si) and experiences the architect as the problem. Neither is wrong about their criterion — the resolution is translation: the architect learns to frame improvements in human-impact terms, the manager learns to hear critique of the process as care for the outcome.
One of them must be mistyped.
The INTJ should be fired.
The manager should defer to the architect.
scenarios.hint: An INTJ and ESFJ collide over process vs people — what is the type-level reading?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It reads both positions as legitimate criterion-differences (Ni-Te vs Fe-Si) and prescribes mutual translation rather than picking a winner — the mature use of type in conflict. B/C/D all collapse the dialectic.

scenarios.title: The Burned-Out Advocate
scenarios.situation: An INFJ counselor has absorbed clients' pain for years, never sets boundaries, and is now burned out — but feels guilty about 'abandoning' people by resting.
evidence: years absorbing clients' pain; guilt about resting; burnout.
choices: Ni-Fe's characteristic failure mode: Fe's other-focus plus Ni's idealistic vision, without the thinking-function boundaries (the impersonal 'no,' the sustainable structure). The guilt is Fi-shadow material — the values turned inward as self-punishment. The prescription: develop the thinking functions (boundaries as logic: 'I help more people over 30 years rested than 3 years burned out') and treat rest as ethical, not selfish.
INFJs can't do counseling.
More empathy will fix it.
Burnout is weakness.
scenarios.hint: An INFJ counselor burns out from boundaryless empathy — what is the analysis?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It diagnoses the specific stack failure mode (Fe without thinking-boundaries), reframes the guilt, and gives the thinking-function prescription with the sustainability logic — development, not type-change. B/C/D all mishandle.

scenarios.title: The Dismissed Warning
scenarios.situation: An ISTJ operations veteran warns that the new 'disruptive' initiative will break compliance. The intuitive leadership team dismisses it as 'resistance to change.' Six months later, the compliance failure costs millions.
evidence: dismissed warning; 6 months later: multimillion compliance failure.
choices: The SJ blind spot runs both ways: leadership dismissed Si's precedent-based warning as mere resistance — but Si is institutional memory, and 'we've seen this fail' is data. The lesson isn't 'Sentinels are always right' (their unprecedented-blind spot is real) but that dismissing the precedent-keeper's warning without investigation is the N-bias failure mode. The process fix: every disruptive proposal gets the Si review — 'what does precedent say?' — as a formal gate.
Sentinels are always right.
Intuition beats experience.
The veteran should have adapted silently.
scenarios.hint: An ISTJ's compliance warning is dismissed as 'resistance' — then proves right — what is the lesson?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It holds both truths (Si's warning was data; the unprecedented-blind spot is still real) and gives the structural fix (formal Si-review gate) — the N-bias correction without overcorrection. B overcorrects; C restates the bias; D silences the function.

scenarios.title: The Crisis and the Report
scenarios.situation: An ESTP technician resolves a critical outage in 20 brilliant improvised minutes — then won't write the incident report. The outage recurs a month later because no one documented the fix.
evidence: 20-minute improvised fix; no report; recurrence in a month.
choices: Honor the gift (crisis virtuosity is rare and valuable) while scaffolding the blind spot (the longer arc): pair the ESTP with a documenting partner, make the debrief immediate and verbal (Se-friendly capture), and frame documentation as 'future-you's tool' not bureaucracy. The prescription adds the missing orientation without punishing the present-tense genius.
ESTPs can't do documentation.
Punish the missing report.
Improvisation is the problem.
scenarios.hint: An ESTP's brilliant fix goes undocumented and the outage recurs — what is the prescription?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It protects the asset (crisis virtuosity) while building the specific scaffold (immediate verbal debrief, documenting partner, future-you framing) — the SP development pattern. B fatalizes; C punishes; D attacks the gift.

scenarios.title: The 'Incompatible' Pair
scenarios.situation: A couple (INTJ + ESFP — all letters flipped) is told by a type forum they're 'incompatible opposites.' They've been happily married for a decade.
evidence: INTJ + ESFP; forum: 'incompatible'; reality: 10 happy years.
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with the forum's claim?
choices: The 'opposite' framing mistakes structural complement for enmity: INTJ (Ni-Se) and ESFP (Se-Ni) share the same perceiving axis in reverse — each supplies what the other underuses, which is fascination and growth material, not incompatibility. Ten happy years are the empirical rebuttal; the forum confused a simplification with a law.
The forum is right; they're mistyped.
Opposites always fail eventually.
One of them must be unhappy secretly.
scenarios.hint: An 'incompatible opposite' couple is happy for a decade — what is wrong with the claim?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It gives the function-level account (shared axis, reversed — complement not enmity) and lets the empirical evidence (ten happy years) rebut the forum's law-claim. B/C/D all deny the data to save the theory.

scenarios.title: The Colleague Diagnosis
scenarios.situation: A manager starts labeling team members by type in meetings: 'That's such an ISTJ thing to say.' The labeled colleagues feel reduced and mocked.
evidence: manager: 'such an ISTJ thing to say' (smirking); colleagues feel reduced.
scenarios.prompt: What is the violation and the correction?
choices: The ethical line: unconsented public typing becomes a cage/dismissal — 'such an ISTJ thing' reduces the person to the label and, said with a smirk, mocks. The correction: type is for private understanding and invited discussion, never for labeling others aloud. The manager should apologize, stop the labels, and use any type insight silently (e.g., giving the ISTJ the detailed brief they prefer).
Typing colleagues is fine.
The colleagues are too sensitive.
Ban all type discussion at work.
scenarios.hint: A manager labels colleagues by type aloud; they feel mocked — what is the violation and correction?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It names the violation (unconsented labeling as reduction/mockery), gives the rule (private/invited only), the repair (apologize, stop), and the legitimate alternative (silent use). B/C endorse the violation; D overcorrects.

domains.name: Temperament Theory
domains.description: Keirsey's temperaments, interaction styles, and the deeper groupings behind the letters.

scenarios.title: The Unclear Letters
scenarios.situation: A test-taker's letters are borderline on three scales, but they answer 'what do you crave?' instantly: 'to understand how things really work and master them.'
evidence: 3 borderline scales; instant answer: 'understand and master.'
choices: A clear Rational (NT) temperament despite unclear letters: the motivational drive is often more accessible to introspection than the cognitive preferences — 'what do you crave?' bypasses the item-level confusion. The temperament gives the practitioner the working hypothesis (NT family) while the letters stay provisional. This is Keirsey's diagnostic value in action.
The test failed.
Craving is irrelevant.
Assign NT arbitrarily.
scenarios.hint: Borderline letters but an instant 'mastery' craving — what does this indicate?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It explains why the drive-question works (motivation is introspectively accessible) and gives the proper use (working hypothesis, letters provisional) — Keirsey complementing Myers. B/C dismiss; D is arbitrary.

scenarios.title: The Meeting Misfire
scenarios.situation: A Chart-the-Course manager (INTJ) runs meetings by cold-calling for instant opinions; the Behind-the-Scenes team (INTPs, ISFPs) goes silent and disengages.
evidence: cold-call meetings; Behind-the-Scenes team silent, disengaged.
choices: Align the process with the styles: send the agenda and questions beforehand (Chart-the-Course preparation need honored AND it serves Behind-the-Scenes reflection), collect initial input in writing, then discuss. The silence isn't disagreement — it's the reflective styles' process need unmet. The fix costs nothing and recovers the team's best thinking.
The team is disengaged; replace them.
Cold-calling builds toughness.
Cancel meetings entirely.
scenarios.hint: Cold-called reflective types go silent — what is the style-level fix?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It diagnoses the silence as unmet process need (not disengagement) and gives the zero-cost fix (pre-reads + written input) that serves both styles. B/C misdiagnose; D avoids.

scenarios.title: The 'New' Discovery
scenarios.situation: A pop-psychology author announces a 'revolutionary discovery': people fall into four motivational groups — Drivers, Builders, Connectors, Visionaries — with no mention of prior work.
choices: The pattern is ancient, the labels are new: four-fold motivational groupings run from Hippocrates through Keirsey — the author's 'discovery' is a relabeling without lineage. The response isn't dismissal (the pattern keeps reappearing because it points at something real) but attribution: show the lineage, ask what the new labels add in machinery or evidence, and judge the book by its incremental contribution, not its revolutionary marketing.
It's a genuine breakthrough.
Four-group theories are all worthless.
Rebranding is harmless.
scenarios.hint: A 'revolutionary' four-group theory ignores all prior work — what is the accurate response?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It places the claim in the 2,400-year lineage, neither dismisses the recurring pattern nor credits the marketing, and gives the evaluation standard (incremental contribution). B buys the hype; C discards the pattern; D excuses the erasure.

scenarios.title: The 'Difficult' Child
scenarios.situation: A 9-year-old SP-temperament boy is labeled 'difficult' and 'disruptive' in a highly regimented SJ-style classroom — desk-bound, silent, routine-drilled. Punishments escalate; behavior worsens.
evidence: 9-year-old SP; desk-bound SJ classroom; escalating punishments.
scenarios.prompt: What is the temperament reading and intervention?
choices: Temperament-environment mismatch, not misbehavior: the Artisan drive (movement, hands-on, freedom within bounds) is being starved systematically by the desk-bound regimen — the 'disruption' is the drive seeking outlet. The intervention is environmental: hands-on learning blocks, movement breaks, choice within structure, a role that uses his energy (the class builder/fixer). Punishment escalates the starvation; the environment change feeds the drive.
The child is difficult; more discipline.
The child is broken; assess pathology.
Remove the child from school.
scenarios.hint: An SP boy is 'difficult' in a regimented classroom — what is the reading and intervention?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It reframes misbehavior as starvation, gives the environmental prescription (hands-on, movement, choice, role), and explains why punishment backfires — the mismatch analysis applied. B/C pathologize or punish; D abandons.

scenarios.title: The Merger
scenarios.situation: An NT startup (move fast, break things, mastery-driven) is acquired by an SJ corporation (continuity, process, duty-driven). Six months in, both sides call the other incompetent — the startup sees bureaucracy, the corporation sees recklessness.
choices: Name the drive collision (mastery vs continuity) and stop the competence framing — both sides are competent at their drive's game. The structural fix: the pilot zone (the startup operates as the corporation's R&D lab — NT experiment inside SJ guardrails: budget caps, compliance gates, brand boundaries), with explicit translation rituals (the 'why this process exists' briefings for NTs; the 'what the experiment taught' briefings for SJs). The merger's value IS the clash managed — innovation with continuity.
The startup must fully assimilate.
The corporation must get out of the way.
The merger was a mistake; unwind it.
scenarios.hint: An NT startup and SJ acquirer call each other incompetent — what is the intervention?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It de-moralizes (drive collision, not incompetence), designs the pilot-zone structure feeding both drives, and adds the translation rituals — the protocol at organizational scale. B/C suppress one side; D abandons the value.

scenarios.title: The Unclear Executive
scenarios.situation: An executive's letters are borderline on all four scales — but their life record shows: fights for competence relentlessly, bored rigid by routine operations, chose the hardest technical challenges at every free choice, admires master engineers.
evidence: fights for competence; bored by routine; free choices all technical mastery.
choices: Clear Rational (NT) by triangulation: the conflict test (fights for competence), boredom test (routine operations = kryptonite), and life record (free choices all mastery-seeking) converge — four of five indicators point NT regardless of the borderline letters. The letters measured the instrument's uncertainty; the drives measured the person. Verdict: NT temperament, letters provisional — and the career implications (mastery-driven roles, competence cultures) follow the hunger.
Borderline letters mean no temperament.
Pick the letters' slight lean.
Retake until the letters are clear.
scenarios.hint: Borderline letters but a mastery-driven life record — what is the verdict?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It runs the triangulation explicitly (conflict, boredom, record converging), distinguishes instrument-uncertainty from person-clarity, and draws the practical implication — the method demonstrated. B/C/D all surrender to the letters.

domains.name: Type Dynamics & the Stack
domains.description: The function stack in motion: positions, loops, grips, stress, and lifespan development.

scenarios.title: The Unexpected Sentimentality
scenarios.situation: An INTJ executive — all strategy and systems — is discovered tearing up at a team's farewell speech, then is embarrassed and dismissive: 'I don't know what came over me.'
evidence: INTJ executive tearing up at farewell; embarrassed, dismissive.
choices: Tertiary Fi surfacing: the INTJ's third function (introverted feeling) is the relief/inferior-adjacent position — genuine but less mature, emerging in unguarded moments. The embarrassment is the Te-dominant's discomfort with the less-controlled function. The reading normalizes it (it's part of the stack, not a malfunction) and points to development: befriending tertiary Fi is the INTJ's midlife work.
The executive is mistyped.
Emotion is malfunction.
INTJs can't feel.
scenarios.hint: An INTJ's unguarded sentimentality embarrasses them — what is the stack reading?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It places the moment precisely (tertiary Fi, relief position) and turns it into development direction (befriending the tertiary) rather than anomaly or mistype. B/C/D all pathologize or deny.

scenarios.title: The Withdrawn Certainty
scenarios.situation: An INTJ founder under funding stress stops listening to the team, retreats into vision-documents, and makes value-laden pronouncements about who's 'aligned.' The Te reality-checks (metrics, feedback) are gone.
evidence: funding stress; vision-docs; 'alignment' pronouncements; no metrics.
scenarios.prompt: What is happening and what breaks it?
choices: Ni-Fi loop: the dominant (vision) and tertiary (values) spinning without the auxiliary (Te) — withdrawn certainty, pronouncements without reality-checks. What breaks it is deliberately re-engaging Te: the metrics review, the customer calls, the boring operational list — the auxiliary's reality-contact restores the balance the loop bypassed. The founder doesn't need a new vision; they need the missing function.
The founder needs a new vision.
The team should comply.
Introversion is the problem.
scenarios.hint: A stressed INTJ founder loops into withdrawn certainty — what is happening and what breaks it?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It diagnoses the loop precisely (Ni-Fi bypassing Te) and prescribes the specific recovery (deliberate Te re-engagement) — the repair-manual use of the stack. B/C/D all miss the mechanism.

scenarios.title: The 'Wrong' Stressed Result
scenarios.situation: An ENFP under chronic work stress tests as ISTJ: detail-obsessed, rigid, anxious about procedures — utterly unlike their usual spontaneous, possibility-loving self.
evidence: ENFP, chronic stress; tests ISTJ: rigid, detail-anxious.
choices: Si-grip masquerading as type: under chronic stress the inferior (Si) seizes control — obsessive detail-review, procedural anxiety, the uncharacteristic rigidity. The ISTJ result measures the grip state, not the personality. The remedy: recover first (rest, the stressor addressed), retest in calm, and use best-fit — the spontaneous self is the data; the stressed result is the artifact.
They've become an ISTJ.
The first test was wrong.
Stress reveals the true type.
scenarios.hint: A stressed ENFP tests as ISTJ — what is the explanation?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It identifies the grip mechanism (inferior Si seized), distinguishes state from trait, and gives the remedy sequence (recover, retest in calm, best-fit) — the full professional handling. B/C/D all confuse state with trait.

scenarios.title: The 'Late' Developer
scenarios.situation: A 45-year-old INTP worries their type is 'wrong' because they're now organized, socially skilled, and decisive — 'INTPs aren't like this.'
choices: Healthy stack development, not mistype: by midlife the auxiliary (Ne, now fluent), tertiary (Si, maturing into reliability), and even inferior (Fe, developing social attunement) have grown — the 45-year-old INTP is the same type with a developed stack. The letters describe the preference order, not a permanent skill ceiling. This is individuation working as designed.
They're mistyped; reassign.
Development is impossible; the type is fixed.
They were never INTP.
scenarios.hint: A 45-year-old INTP is now organized and socially skilled — is the type wrong?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It reads the growth as the developmental sequence working (auxiliary fluent, tertiary maturing, inferior developing) and reaffirms the letters as preference order, not skill ceiling. B/C/D all deny development.

scenarios.title: The Two Strategists
scenarios.situation: An INTJ strategist (Ni-dom: 'the vision is clear, commit') clashes with an ENTP strategist (Ne-dom: 'the options are open, explore') over the company's direction. Each thinks the other is strategically incompetent.
evidence: INTJ: 'commit to the vision' vs ENTP: 'keep options open.'
choices: Dominant-function collision: the Ni-dom converges (one vision, commit — deviation feels like dilution) while the Ne-dom branches (options open, explore — commitment feels like blindness). Both are strategizing correctly BY THEIR DOMINANT — the incompetence charge is the fluency fallacy (my leading function is strategy itself). The resolution: sequence them — Ne's option-generation first (the exploration phase), Ni's convergence second (the commitment phase) — the strategy process that uses both dominants in order.
One of them is wrong about strategy.
Ni beats Ne (or vice versa).
Strategists shouldn't collaborate.
scenarios.hint: Ni-dom and Ne-dom strategists call each other incompetent — what is the reading?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It names the collision mechanistically (converge vs branch), diagnoses the fallacy (fluency = strategy itself), and sequences the process (explore then commit) — both dominants honored in order. B/C pick a winner; D avoids.

scenarios.title: The Meltdown Protocol
scenarios.situation: A team lead notices a normally visionary INTJ colleague binge-eating, impulse-shopping, and making reckless decisions — uncharacteristic and compulsive. The lead's instinct is a performance warning.
evidence: visionary INTJ: bingeing, impulse-shopping, reckless -- uncharacteristic.
choices: Recognize the Se-grip signature (uncharacteristic + compulsive = inferior eruption, not performance failure) and respond with the protocol, not punishment: reduce demand quietly, offer genuine support ('you don't seem yourself — what would help?'), avoid the performance framing (it deepens the siege), and address the stressor privately once the episode passes. The grip is the alarm — the lead's job is hearing it, and the help-signal awareness if it persists.
Issue the performance warning.
Ignore it; it's personal.
Tell the team to work around them.
scenarios.hint: A colleague's uncharacteristic compulsive behavior — warning or protocol?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It identifies the grip (not performance failure), gives the humane response sequence (reduce demand, genuine support, no performance framing, address stressor after), and keeps the help-signal awareness — the protocol applied managerially. B punishes the alarm; C/D abdicate.

domains.name: Taking the Assessment Well
domains.description: How the Humanmetrics instrument works and how to answer honestly for an accurate result.

scenarios.title: The 'Both' Complaint
scenarios.situation: A test-taker protests: 'Every question made me choose, but I'm both! The test is flawed — it should allow both.'
evidence: 'every question forced a choice, but I'm both!'
choices: The forced choice is the method, not a flaw: allowing 'both' would let the aspirational or situational self hide — the constraint forces the habitual pattern to declare itself, which is exactly what a preference instrument needs to measure. 'Both' is often true (everyone uses both orientations) but uninformative; the forced pick reveals which is habitual. The frustration is the instrument working.
The test is flawed; allow both.
The test-taker has no preferences.
Skip those items.
scenarios.hint: A test-taker protests forced choices — 'I'm both!' — what is the accurate response?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It explains the psychometric rationale (constraint reveals habit; 'both' is true but uninformative) and reframes the frustration as the method working. B/C/D all misunderstand the design.

scenarios.title: The Crisis Result
scenarios.situation: A test-taker completes the assessment during the worst week of their life (job loss, grief) and gets a dramatically different result from their historical type.
evidence: worst week: job loss + grief; result differs dramatically.
choices: Treat it as state, not trait: the crisis week's answers measured the stress response (likely grip-influenced), not the habitual preferences. Note the result with interest (it reveals the stress signature), recover, and retest in calm — this is state-hygiene retesting, the principled kind, not clarity-shopping. The historical type, confirmed by best-fit, stands until calm-state evidence says otherwise.
The new result is the true self; crisis reveals truth.
Average the two results.
Never trust any result again.
scenarios.hint: A crisis-week result differs dramatically from the historical type — what should they do?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It applies the state/trait distinction, finds value in the crisis result (stress-signature data), and gives the principled retest protocol — distinguishing hygiene from clarity-shopping. B romanticizes crisis; C averages noise; D abandons.

scenarios.title: The Flattering Description

scenarios.situation: A startup's founding team is four NTs. They're brilliant, fast, and six months in, they have no users — the product is elegant and nobody wants it.

The engineer is mistyped.
Talent doesn't matter; fit does.

INFPs can't be executives.
Quit immediately.

scenarios.situation: An INTJ founder's Ni runs unchecked — grand visions, no Te execution: the team drifts, the runway burns, the vision documents pile up.

Abandon growth.

lessons.title: Self-Knowledge: The Humanmetrics Assessment — Core concepts
concepts: The instrument: a questionnaire sorting preferences across four dichotomies — Extraversion/Introversion (energy source), Sensing/Intuition (information intake), Thinking/Feeling (decision basis), Judging/Perceiving (orientation to the outer world) — into 16 types. The percentages report preference clarity, not grades.

The 16 types are working styles, not worth ranks: each type names a characteristic pattern of energy, attention, and decision-making. No type is better; each has characteristic strengths and characteristic blind spots.

What it measures: preferences — stable-ish tendencies in how you prefer to work. What it doesn't: ability, intelligence, skills, motivation, mental health, or future job performance. Preference is not competence.

Career-fit mapping uses type to predict energy cost, not to grant permission: match working style to role-family demands (structure vs. ambiguity, people vs. systems, closure vs. exploration) to find roles that energize rather than drain.

Team composition: complementary working styles cover more ground than uniform ones. The typology's team value is predictive — naming friction points (independence vs. process, big-picture vs. detail) so the team designs around them.

The development plan: identify the non-preferred functions your goals demand, build them with deliberate low-stakes reps and observable markers, and lead from your strengths while the weaker side catches up.

example.walkthrough: Each dichotomy is a tug-of-war between its two poles; the winner is the preferred side and the margin — expressed as a percentage — is the preference clarity. The 40.0 next to 'I' mirrors the scenario's 'Introverted (38%)': a moderate signal. A 3% margin would warn you to read both neighboring type descriptions, exactly as the lesson advises.

pitfalls: Common trap: treating the four letters as a verdict. The percentages are the actual information — a 3% preference is a near-tie, and the label alone misleads.
Common trap: using preferences as a hiring filter. The instrument measures how people prefer to work, not whether they can do the work — gating on type is misuse.
Common trap: letting type forbid ambition. Mapping predicts energy cost and friction; it never determines what you're allowed to attempt or achieve.
Common trap: confusing the map with the territory. The 16 boxes are a vocabulary for reflection, not a scientific verdict on your potential — pair them with skills audits and real-world feedback.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

lessons.title: Jung's Psychological Types: The 1921 Origin
concepts: Carl Jung published Psychological Types in 1921 after breaking with Freud — the book that introduced extraversion/introversion and the psychological functions (thinking, feeling, sensation, intuition) to the world. Jung wasn't building a test; he was mapping how consciousness orients itself, drawn from clinical observation and his own self-analysis.

Jung's core claim: people differ systematically in how they perceive (sensation vs intuition) and judge (thinking vs feeling), and in their attitude toward the world (extraversion vs introversion). These aren't abilities — everyone uses all functions — but preferences: the habitual, energizing modes versus the effortful ones. The Humanmetrics test operationalizes these preferences as four dichotomies.

The historical path to the test: Katharine Briggs and Isabel Myers (mother and daughter) read Jung and built the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator to make his theory practically usable — first for wartime workforce placement, later for counseling and teams. The Humanmetrics Jung Typology Test is an independent, freely available instrument in the same Jungian lineage, using forced-choice items to estimate the four preferences.

Why the origin matters for test-takers: the assessment measures preferences, not skills, intelligence, or worth. 'I prefer introversion' says where you recharge, not what you can do. Every misinterpretation of type results — as destiny, as ability ranking, as excuse — violates this founding distinction.

example.code:
Jung (1921) -> Briggs & Myers -> MBTI instrument
                \-> Humanmetrics Jung Typology Test (free, online)
Core distinction: PREFERENCE (habitual, energizing) vs ABILITY
  preference: where you orient naturally (e.g., toward inner world)
  ability:    what you can do (everyone can act extraverted)
The test estimates the four preferences:
  E/I (attitude) + S/N (perceiving) + T/F (judging) + J/P (lifestyle)
example.walkthrough: The lineage diagram places the Humanmetrics test in its intellectual history — Jung's theory, the Briggs-Myers operationalization, and the free Humanmetrics instrument as one branch. The preference-vs-ability distinction is the load-bearing concept: everything the test reports is a preference estimate, and every misuse (as ability ranking or destiny) violates this founding distinction.

pitfalls: Reading type as ability: 'I'm an INTP so I can't do sales' — preferences describe energy economics, not capability ceilings.
Treating the test as Jung's own: Jung never built an instrument — the test is an operationalization two steps removed; know the lineage.
Ignoring the clinical origins: the theory came from observing real psychological differences, not from a quiz-design brainstorm — respect the source.
lessons.try_it: Read a summary of Jung's definitions of extraversion and introversion (Chapter X of Psychological Types, in summary). Write 200 words on how his definitions differ from the pop-culture 'shy vs outgoing' version.

lessons.title: Attitudes: Extraversion & Introversion
concepts: Jung's attitude describes where psychic energy flows: extraversion orients toward the outer world (people, activity, the environment), introversion toward the inner world (ideas, reflection, depth). The extravert recharges by engaging; the introvert recharges by withdrawing. It's an energy economy, not a social skill rating — introverts can be brilliant presenters, extraverts can be deep thinkers.

The Humanmetrics E/I scale estimates this preference through forced-choice items about typical behavior ('at parties, you usually...'). Scores near the middle indicate flexibility or situational variation, not a failed test — the preference is a tendency, and many people operate near the border, drawing on both orientations as context demands.

Workplace implications are practical, not moral: extraverts tend to think aloud, prefer collaborative processing, and may find long solitary stretches draining; introverts tend to think before speaking, prefer written or small-group processing, and may find back-to-back meetings depleting. Neither is better — but teams that honor both get the thinking-aloud energy and the considered reflection.

The common distortions: equating introversion with shyness or social anxiety (they're independent — confident introverts exist), equating extraversion with superficiality, and treating the preference as fixed forever (preferences are stable but not immutable; life develops both). The test reports a preference snapshot, not a life sentence.

example.code:
E/I: the energy economy
  EXTRAVERSION (E) .... orients outward; recharges via engagement;
     thinks aloud; breadth-first processing; drained by isolation.
  INTROVERSION (I) .... orients inward; recharges via withdrawal;
     thinks before speaking; depth-first processing; drained by
     crowds.
  Both: everyone uses both; preference = the habitual,
  energizing mode. Mid-range scores = flexibility, not failure.
example.walkthrough: The energy-economy framing (recharge source, processing style, drain conditions) replaces the pop-culture shy/outgoing caricature with Jung's actual construct. The 'both' note is the critical qualifier — preference as habitual mode, mid-range as flexibility — which prevents the test result from becoming an identity cage.

pitfalls: Introversion = shyness: social anxiety is independent of the attitude — confident introverts and anxious extraverts both exist.
Treating E/I as skill: 'extraverts are better leaders' — the preference predicts energy patterns, not competence; leadership skill is separate.
Mid-range scores as 'wrong': near-middle means flexible or situational — a valid result, not a test failure.
lessons.try_it: Track your energy for three days: note which activities recharge vs drain you, and whether the pattern matches your E/I result. Write 200 words on the fit.

lessons.title: The Four Functions: Thinking, Feeling, Sensation, Intuition
concepts: Jung's functions are the psyche's operations, in two pairs. The perceiving functions gather information: Sensation (what is — concrete, present, factual) versus Intuition (what could be — patterns, possibilities, the future). The judging functions decide: Thinking (impersonal logic — true/false, consistent/inconsistent) versus Feeling (personal values — good/bad, harmonious/discordant).

The critical clarification: Jung's 'feeling' is not emotion — it's a rational judging function that evaluates by values, as systematic in its way as thinking's logic. And 'thinking' isn't intelligence — it's the preference for impersonal criteria. The pop-culture mapping (thinking = smart, feeling = emotional) is exactly backwards from Jung's technical meanings.

Everyone uses all four functions; the type describes the habitual hierarchy — which leads (dominant), which assists (auxiliary), and which are less developed. The Humanmetrics S/N and T/F scales estimate the preferred perceiving and judging functions respectively. A 'T' preference means thinking leads judgments, not that feeling is absent.

Why functions matter more than letters: two people with the same four letters can differ enormously if their function stacks differ in development — and the dynamics domain will show how the stack (dominant through inferior) explains behavior the letters alone can't. The letters are the address; the functions are the residents.

example.code:
Jung's four functions (two pairs)
  PERCEIVING (gathering info):
    Sensation .... what IS: concrete, present, factual, trusted senses
    Intuition .... what COULD BE: patterns, possibilities, future
  JUDGING (deciding):
    Thinking ..... impersonal logic: true/false, consistent/inconsistent
    Feeling ...... personal values: good/bad, harmonious/discordant
                   (NOT emotion -- a rational valuing function)
  Everyone uses all four; type = the habitual hierarchy.
example.walkthrough: The two-pair structure (perceiving vs judging) with the technical definitions replaces the pop-culture caricatures — especially the feeling/emotion correction, which is the single most common misunderstanding. The hierarchy note (everyone uses all four; type is the ordering) sets up the dynamics domain, and the address/residents metaphor makes the letters-functions relationship memorable.

pitfalls: Feeling = emotional: Jung's feeling is rational evaluation by values — conflating it with emotion insults both feelers and the theory.
Thinking = smart: the preference is for impersonal criteria, not cognitive ability — brilliant feelers and muddled thinkers exist.
One-function identities: 'I'm a thinker' as if the other three don't operate — the hierarchy includes all four; type is the ordering.
lessons.try_it: For one recent decision you made, identify which function led (data-gathering: S or N? deciding: T or F?) and which assisted. Write 200 words on the hierarchy you observe in yourself.

lessons.title: Persona & Shadow: The Whole Self
concepts: Beyond the four letters, Jung mapped the psyche's architecture: the persona (the social mask — the face we present, necessary and healthy in its place), the ego (the conscious 'I'), and the shadow (the disowned parts — qualities we've rejected, both 'negative' like aggression and 'positive' like unclaimed creativity). Type describes the ego's habitual preferences; the shadow holds what the preferences exclude.

The type-shadow relationship: a strong Thinking preference often shadows Feeling (values dismissed as 'irrational'), a strong Judging preference shadows spontaneity. The inferior function (the dynamics domain's topic) lives at the shadow's border — under stress, it erupts in characteristic ways (the Thinker's uncharacteristic emotional outburst, the Planner's chaotic binge).

Why this matters for self-knowledge: the test reports the preferred, conscious side — but wholeness (Jung's individuation) requires befriending the shadow, not just polishing the persona. 'I'm an INTJ' as a complete identity misses the disowned parts that drive the person's actual problems. The assessment is a starting map, not the territory.

Practical shadow work (psychological, not mystical): notice disproportionate reactions (intense irritation at someone's 'illogical' emotion may be your own disowned feeling), journal the traits you condemn in others, and ask what the rejected quality is protecting. This is the depth dimension the four letters point toward but don't contain.

example.code:
The psyche's architecture (Jung)
  PERSONA .... the social mask (necessary; pathological only when
                 mistaken for the whole self)
  EGO ........ the conscious 'I'; type describes its preferences
  SHADOW ..... the disowned: rejected qualities ('negative' AND
                 'positive' -- unclaimed strengths too)
  Type-shadow link: the inferior function borders the shadow;
  under stress it erupts (the Thinker's outburst, the J's chaos).
  Individuation = befriending the shadow, not polishing the persona.
example.walkthrough: The architecture diagram places type correctly — as the ego's preferences, one layer among several — with the persona/shadow framing that gives self-knowledge its depth.
