Analyze: best-fit with considered alternatives and why-nots; stack map with two dated examples per position; stress signature with documented episodes.
Apply: the translated relationship (before/after); the environment audit (starved/fed + change).
Plan: the lifelong curriculum — scheduled practices, the inferior invitation, annual retest date, review cadence.
Review: run the Barnum protocol on your own portfolio — cut or evidence every surviving claim.

checks.hint: The why-nots are load-bearing: 'why not ENTJ' with reasons beats 'why INTJ' alone.
Two dated examples per stack position — the territory, not the legend.
The Barnum self-review is the quality gate; no portfolio ships without it.

labs.success_message: A complete, evidence-grade portfolio: analyzed, applied, planned, and self-reviewed.

sections.title: Self-Knowledge: The Humanmetrics Assessment — Core path

behavioral.prompt: Describe your working style in two minutes — how you recharge, decide, and organize work.
points: Name your preferences plainly (energy source, decision basis, planning style) with the assessment as vocabulary, not scripture
Give one concrete work example proving each preference
Close with what this means for a team: what you contribute and what support helps you thrive
pitfalls: Reciting four letters with no examples
Presenting preferences as fixed destiny
Only strengths, no blind spots

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you adapted your working style to a teammate who worked very differently.
points: Describe the difference concretely (their style vs. yours) without caricature
Show the specific adaptation: what you changed in communication, planning, or feedback
Name the outcome for the work and what you kept from the experience
pitfalls: Implying their style was wrong and yours was right
A vague 'we communicated better' with no specifics
No lasting change described

behavioral.prompt: What is your biggest working-style blind spot, and how do you manage it?
points: Name the blind spot precisely, tied to your profile (e.g., impatience with process, conflict avoidance)
Show the system that compensates: checklists, scheduled reviews, an accountability partner
Give evidence the system works — a time it caught what you would have missed
pitfalls: A humblebrag blind spot ('I work too hard')
Awareness with no compensating system
Blaming the blind spot for a real failure without owning it

behavioral.prompt: How do you handle conflict with someone whose decision style is the opposite of yours?
points: Show you translate first: restate their position in their decision language (values vs. logic)
Describe separating the people from the problem: shared criteria before positions
Name a real example and the decision mechanism you used
pitfalls: Avoiding conflict entirely
Winning the argument as the goal
No real example

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you led through ambiguity — no clear plan, shifting requirements.
points: Set the ambiguity honestly: what was unknown and what was at stake
Show your method for creating clarity: time-boxed exploration, reversible decisions, explicit assumptions
Name what the team needed from you emotionally, not just technically
pitfalls: Pretending you had a plan all along
Ignoring the human side of ambiguity
No method — just endurance

behavioral.prompt: How do you recharge, and how do you protect that in a demanding role?
points: Name your actual recharge pattern (solitude, people, movement, making things)
Show the boundary system: calendar blocks, rituals, non-negotiables
Connect it to performance: how protected recovery makes your work better
pitfalls: 'I don't need recharge' machismo
No concrete boundary system
Treating rest as weakness

behavioral.prompt: Describe a development goal you're actively working on — a weaker side you're building.
points: Name the specific capability and why your goals demand it
Describe the deliberate reps: frequency, stakes, feedback source
Give the observable marker you'll use to know it's working
pitfalls: A vague goal like 'be more empathetic' with no reps
No marker for progress
Working on a strength and calling it development

behavioral.prompt: Why does self-knowledge matter for the role you're pursuing?
points: Tie specific role demands to your working style honestly — where you fit naturally and where you'll stretch
Show the team value: how your self-knowledge makes you easier to work with
Name what you're still learning about yourself — curiosity over completion
pitfalls: Generic 'self-awareness is important' with no role connection
Claiming perfect fit with no stretch areas
Using the assessment as a credential rather than a mirror

cheatsheet.title: Self-Knowledge: The Humanmetrics Assessment — field reference

sections.heading: The four dichotomies
items: E/I: where you get energy — outer world vs. inner world
S/N: how you take in information — concrete facts vs. patterns
T/F: how you decide — impersonal logic vs. human values
J/P: how you orient outward — closure and plans vs. openness and spontaneity

sections.heading: Reading a result
items: Below ~15% clarity: read the neighboring type too
The letters are shorthand; the full profile is the instrument

sections.heading: Scope discipline
items: Measures: preferences. Does not measure: ability, skill, performance
Use for: self-knowledge, energy management, team design, development
Never for: hiring filters, promotions, worth judgments

sections.heading: From type to plan
items: Map type -> role-family energy fit (friction forecast, not permission)
Compose teams for complementary coverage; name friction early
Develop non-preferred functions with reps + observable markers

glossary.def: A personality framework sorting preferences across four dichotomies into 16 types, originating in Carl Jung's psychological types.
The percentage strength of a reported preference on one dichotomy; low clarity means both sides' descriptions may apply.
The characteristic pattern of energy, attention, and decision-making a type describes — how someone prefers to work.
Whether a person primarily gains energy from the outer world of people and action or the inner world of reflection.
Whether decisions primarily rest on impersonal logic and criteria or on human values and impact.
Whether a person prefers closure, plans, and decidedness or openness, spontaneity, and keeping options open in outer life.
The characteristic weakness of a type — the non-preferred functions it tends to neglect under pressure.
The sides of each dichotomy a person uses less naturally; the target of deliberate development.

simulations.title: The 51/49 split
simulations.brief: A candidate scores 51/49 on Extraversion/Introversion and the hiring manager wants a label. Hold the line on honesty.

steps.symptom: A candidate scores 51% Extraversion / 49% Introversion. The hiring manager wants a label.
options: Report a slight preference for Extraversion — near-ties are the instrument saying 'unclear', not a type verdict
steps.explain: Humanmetrics reports preference clarity for a reason: 51/49 is within the instrument's noise. Honest reporting says 'slight' and moves on.

steps.symptom: The manager still wants one letter for the org chart.
options: Refuse the false precision: give the full profile with clarity bands — the chart can carry four letters with qualifiers
steps.explain: Collapsing a near-tie to a letter manufactures certainty the data does not contain. The ethical move is the full, qualified profile.

steps.symptom: How do you use a 51/49 result in coaching?
options: Treat it as flexibility: the person draws on both modes — coach the range, not the label
steps.explain: Near-ties are information: this person flexes. Coaching the range beats coaching the label.

simulations.debrief: Close scores are the instrument being honest: report the clarity, refuse false precision, coach the range.

simulations.title: Type is not a trait score
simulations.brief: A manager turns a Thinking preference into a character verdict, then into a hiring filter. Correct both errors.

steps.symptom: A manager says 'She scored 90% Thinking, so she has no empathy.' Correct the category error.
options: Thinking/Feeling is about decision criteria (logic vs values), not capacity for empathy — the inference is invalid
steps.explain: Jungian preferences describe preferred decision-making, not ability or character. T-preference people feel deeply; they just decide differently.

steps.symptom: The manager now wants to use types for hiring filters.
options: Refuse: the instrument was not validated for selection, and type-based hiring is both unethical and legally exposed
steps.explain: Humanmetrics-style instruments lack the validity evidence selection requires, and filtering by type invites adverse-impact liability. Development yes; selection no.

steps.symptom: Where does the instrument legitimately help?
options: Self-knowledge and team communication: a shared vocabulary for working-style differences
steps.explain: The instrument's valid home is development: understanding yourself and adapting to others. Every selection use is out of scope.

simulations.debrief: Know what the instrument is: a preferences lens for growth — never a hiring filter, never a character verdict.

simulations.title: Staff the on-call rotation
simulations.brief: Build a 4-person on-call rotation from type profiles. Use types to inform — and know exactly where their authority ends.

steps.symptom: Build a 4-person on-call rotation from type profiles. What do you optimize for?
options: Coverage of working styles across the rotation: pairing detail-oriented with big-picture, structured with adaptable
steps.explain: Diverse rotations catch more failure modes: the S notices the anomaly, the N sees the pattern, the J follows the runbook, the P improvises.

steps.symptom: Two Sensors want the same holiday week. Resolve it with type-awareness, not favoritism.
evidence: both planned around the holiday months ago
options: A transparent rotation rule decided in advance (seniority/alternation) — type-awareness explains the clash, the rule resolves it
Give it to the louder one
steps.explain: Type language diagnoses (both plan concretely, far ahead); it must not decide. Pre-agreed rules decide — personality never allocates scarce goods.

steps.symptom: The rotation is live. How do you review it?
evidence: page counts, ack times, burnout survey
options: Review outcomes (load fairness, response quality), not types — the roster is judged by results
steps.explain: Staffing decisions are validated by operational outcomes. Type diversity is a hypothesis; page-load fairness is the measurement.

simulations.debrief: Types inform team design; outcomes judge it. Never let a preference label allocate, and always measure the result.

simulations.title: From type to career map
simulations.brief: An INTP analyst asks what roles fit. Map preferences to work modes — and honor the life that contradicts the map.

steps.symptom: An INTP analyst asks what roles fit. Map the preferences, not the stereotype.
evidence: I 80, N 75, T 90, P 65 — all clear
options: Map each preference to work modes: I→deep solo work, N→systems and patterns, T→logic-driven decisions, P→exploratory scope — then match roles to the modes
steps.explain: The honest mapping is preferences → work modes → roles. Stereotype-matching ('INTPs do X') skips the reasoning and bakes in bias.

steps.symptom: They love their current support-desk role despite the 'wrong' type. Response?
evidence: thriving on the desk for 2 years
options: Celebrate it: the instrument describes preferences, not permissions — lived fit beats predicted fit
steps.explain: Reality outranks the model. If someone thrives where the type says they shouldn't, the type description was incomplete — not the person.

steps.symptom: They ask for one practice to grow. What do you prescribe?
options: Deliberate practice in the non-preferred mode (structured facilitation) — type development is range, not prison
steps.explain: Type theory's own growth story is developing the non-preferred functions. Range is the goal; the label is the starting line.

simulations.debrief: Career mapping is preferences → modes → roles, and lived fit always outranks the prediction.

simulations.title: The retest wobble
simulations.brief: INTJ becomes INTP on retest. Explain the wobble with clarity bands — and refuse to narrate identity from noise.

steps.symptom: A candidate retests after 6 months: INTJ → INTP. The J/P flipped. Is the instrument broken?
options: No — near-tie dimensions wobble; the 55/58 flip is the same slight preference measured twice with noise
Test a third time and take the majority
steps.explain: Test-retest reliability is lowest at the middle. A 3-point swing across the line is expected noise, not instrument failure.

steps.symptom: Which dimensions should you trust most in this profile?
options: The high-clarity ones (I, N, T) — clarity bands are the confidence intervals; trust scales with them
steps.explain: Preference-clarity scores are the instrument's own uncertainty bars. Read them as confidence: 90 is a signal, 58 is a shrug.

steps.symptom: The candidate asks what changed about them in 6 months.
options: Probably nothing structural — the wobble is measurement noise on a near-tie; check life context before narrating change
The test was wrong the first time
steps.explain: Do not narrate identity change from a 3-point swing. Ask about life context first; the numbers alone say 'noise'.

simulations.debrief: Retest wobbles are clarity-band physics: trust high-clarity dimensions, shrug at near-ties, and never narrate identity from noise.
